conclusion.label: endorses

report:
Yes, EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) therapy can alleviate the symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Multiple sources confirm it is an evidence-based treatment with strong clinical support.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials examining EMDR's efficacy in PTSD treatment verified its effectiveness, with one meta-analysis of 26 randomized controlled trials involving 1,659 participants showing a large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.08) for reducing PTSD symptoms. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs notes that EMDR is one of the most studied treatments for PTSD and demonstrates effectiveness when administered over approximately 3 months. The American Psychological Association's Clinical Practice Guideline also suggests EMDR for PTSD treatment.

Research indicates that many clients report significant reductions in symptoms, with some studies showing that up to 90% of single-trauma survivors no longer meet PTSD criteria after just three 90-minute sessions. EMDR is widely recognized as an effective, non-invasive treatment for trauma-related conditions and is commonly used in PTSD rehabilitation.

One noted limitation is that the eye movements and bilateral stimulation techniques may not uniquely contribute to EMDR's efficacy—some characterize it as a "purple hat therapy," meaning its effectiveness may stem from therapeutic methods also found in other evidence-based psychotherapies. However, this does not diminish its demonstrated clinical effectiveness.

**Sources:**

- https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/txessentials/emdr_pro.asp
- https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/treatments/eye-movement-reprocessing
- https://gitnux.org/emdr-statistics/
